title: TB9-32140
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): I dismiss this appeal for the reasons that follow.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: I dismiss this appeal for the reasons that follow.

XXXX XXXX XXXX and her sons, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, are citizens of Nigeria. Ms. XXXX and her sons had an initial hearing before the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) in 2017. The RPD rejected their claims. However, the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) granted their appeal later that year. Ms. XXXX claims were re-heard by the RPD in 2019.

Ms. XXXX and her sons fear that, if they return to Nigeria, Ms. XXXX in-laws will kill or seriously harm the sons as a sacrifice because Ms. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. According to Ms. XXXX and her sons, the tradition in her in-laws' family is that the first-born son in the family must be offered up as a sacrifice when a member of the family XXXX XXXX XXXX. For some unknown reason, Ms. XXXX in-laws allegedly insisted that both her sons undergo the rituals. Ms. XXXX also alleges that her spouse's family considers XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and that they would subject her to spiritual cleansing if she returns to Nigeria. According to Ms. XXXX, her family's problems started with the birth of her eldest son but she only became aware of the pressure being placed by her in-laws when he turned XXXX XXXX XXXX. Ms. XXXX, her spouse, and her sons left Nigeria for the United States (US) for a four-week vacation in December XXXX. Ms. XXXX and her family then came to Canada, allegedly for a vacation that same month. Her spouse returned to Nigeria XXXX XXXX2017 after he allegedly received a threatening phone call from his family. Following this, Ms. XXXX applied for refugee protection in Canada. Ms. XXXX spouse returned three times to visit her in Canada in 2018 and 2019 and returned to Nigeria each time. Ms. XXXX alleges that her spouse served her with divorce papers a few months before the RPD's re-determination of this case. Ms. XXXX has not responded to the petition for divorce.

In the decision under appeal, the RPD found that Ms. XXXX testimony was untrustworthy as it found that she could not keep her story straight and, on numerous occasions, her responses were reactive and manufactured. The RPD found that the cumulative effect of all of the credibility concerns set out in its decision was such that it did not have sufficient credible and trustworthy evidence upon which to base a determination that Ms. XXXX and her sons are Convention refugees or persons in need of protection. The RPD also found that Ms. XXXX and her sons have a viable internal flight alternative in Abuja, Enugu and/or Port Harcourt.

My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.1 The RPD was correct in finding that Ms. XXXX and her sons are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection. While I agree with Ms. XXXX counsel that the RPD erred with respect to some of its findings relating to credibility, I find that the findings on which the RPD was correct were sufficient to rebut the presumption of truthfulness that applies in this case. I agree with the RPD that Ms. XXXX account of what led to her and her family to leave Nigeria was not credible, on a balance of probabilities. I also agree with the RPD that Ms. XXXX account of the risk she would face if she and her sons return to Nigeria is not credible. Finally, I agree with the RPD that, in any event, Ms. XXXX and her sons would have viable internal flight alternatives, at the very least, in Abuja, and/or Enugu.

The RAD only has the jurisdiction to hold a hearing in some cases if it has admitted new evidence.2 Ms. XXXX and her sons did not seek to admit any new evidence and therefore their request for an in-person hearing is denied. ANALYSIS Credibility

Counsel for Ms. XXXX and her sons argues that the RPD engaged in a microscopic examination of the issues in this case to arrive at its negative credibility findings. I address each of the arguments made by counsel in detail below. Events when eldest son turned ten

According to Ms. XXXX, her family's horrors began when her eldest son turned ten. However, I agree with the RPD that there were several omissions and inconsistencies in Ms. XXXX evidence regarding the risk that her family began to face at this time.

Counsel argues that an inconsistency in Ms. XXXX evidence regarding the exact source of the risk faced by her sons was simply an omission of peripheral information. I disagree. In the written narrative she submitted with her Basis of Claim form, Ms. XXXX states that her spouse was XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and that he was a candidate XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX of the community. She also states that the threats against her sons arose because her spouse's uncle was the subject of mockery due to the fact that her sons had not undergone certain community rituals. In her written narrative, Ms. XXXX then goes on to talk about threats that her family received from her spouse's uncle.

However, at the hearing, Ms. XXXX testified that the risk her family faced arose from the fact that her spouse's brother XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. She later explained that, when she said uncle she was really referring to her spouse's brother who is older and that, in her culture, no distinction is made between elder brothers and uncles. Even if I accept that this is true, I still agree with the RPD that Ms. XXXX evidence about the source of the risk to her sons was inconsistent as she made no mention of the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX in her written narrative. Instead, as noted above, she referred to her spouse being a candidate for the stool of his community. She also stated that her spouse's uncle (brother) said he had become a subject of mockery among his friends because they thought he could not manage his family and that he might be demoted if the traditional rituals were not performed on Ms. XXXXchildren.

I agree with the RPD that Ms. XXXX failed to provide a satisfactory explanation for this inconsistency in her evidence as she just testified that she was not herself when she wrote her narrative. Her answer as to why she did not include this information in her amended narrative was also not satisfactory as she simply said it did not cross her mind.3 I do not agree with counsel that the exact source or reason for a claimant's risk of persecution is simply a detail. In my view, it is important information that goes to the core of a claim. I also do not agree with counsel that the RPD was engaging in a microscopic examination by focusing on these matters in addition to the other credibility concerns discussed below.

Counsel argued that the RPD erred in subjecting Ms. XXXX to an inappropriate "memory test." I certainly agree with counsel that refugee claims should not be determined on the basis of an inappropriate "memory test." However, I disagree with counsel that the RPD was conducting a memory test when it expected Ms. XXXX to remember significant events and threats that occurred around the time that her eldest son turned ten. In her written narrative, Ms. XXXX stated that, around the time that her eldest son turned ten, her spouse's in-laws insisted that she undergo spiritual cleansing because they saw her XXXX XXXX XXXX. Also, her in-laws visited her house to examine the surroundings in order to determine the best way to attack them.

When the RPD asked Ms. XXXX at the hearing what had occurred around the time that her eldest son turned ten, she failed to mention these significant aspects of her claim, in particular that her in-laws were insisting that she undergo spiritual cleansing because they considered her XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. I do not agree that it was a memory test to expect Ms. XXXX to spontaneously remember this serious threat made to her by her in-laws.

When asked why she had failed to mention this threat in her response to the RPD's questions, Ms. XXXX said that so many things had happened that she could not remember them all.4 I agree with the RPD that being accused of being a witch and being threatened with spiritual cleansing is not a detail one would expect someone to forget, especially since that is the main reason that she personally claimed refugee protection. For these reasons, I agree with the RPD's finding that Ms. XXXX's failure to remember this highly significant threat negatively affected the credibility of her account of events in this case.

For the above reasons, the RPD was correct to find that the above omissions and inconsistencies in Ms. XXXX's evidence regarding the events and threats that occurred around the time her eldest son turned ten had an adverse effect on her credibility. Timing of Ms. XXXX's awareness of her in-laws' demands
I disagree with counsel that the RPD misapprehended Ms. XXXX testimony or erred in any way in its treatment of Ms. XXXX evidence as to when she became aware of the demands being made by her in-laws.

As noted by counsel, Ms. XXXX testified at the hearing that she did not initially know about the demands made by her in-laws that her eldest son undergo certain traditional rituals until her spouse opened up to her about them around the time that her son XXXX XXXX. She testified to this when the RPD asked her why she did not make a claim for asylum in the US.5

However, the problem with this testimony is that, as noted by the RPD, it is inconsistent with the written narrative submitted by Ms. XXXX. In her written narrative, Ms. XXXX stated that her problems with her in-laws began when her eldest son was born as the in-laws claimed that he had to be dedicated to the gods. She then stated: My spouse and I were persistent and steadfast in our prayers and fasting and we believe (sic) that God would protect our son. My spouse and I did not allow them to perform any sacrifice on our son or with our son.6 [emphasis added]

This part of her written narrative clearly implies that she was aware of her in-laws' threats at the time that her eldest son was born as she includes herself in the efforts to pray for him and to disallow the sacrifices.

When asked to explain the inconsistency between her written narrative and her testimony as to when she became aware of the threats being made by her in-laws, Ms. XXXX kept stating that her spouse did not initially tell her about the threats and that she did not know about them until her son XXXX XXXX. She also said that many things happened and that she and her spouse prayed for the safety of their son. I agree with the RPD that these were not satisfactory explanations for the inconsistency between Ms. XXXX's testimony and her written narrative as to when she first found out about the threats being made by her in-laws.

I note further that, although not mentioned by the RPD in its decision, this same inconsistency arose in Ms. XXXX's evidence regarding threats the in-laws made after the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. While Ms. XXXX testified that she was not aware of the threats being made by her in-laws at that time, she states in her written narrative that her spouse's uncle (brother) invited her and her spouse to his village to talk to them about initiating the child. She states in her written narrative that she and her spouse told him that they were not interested and that they believed in Christianity.

When asked about the inconsistency between this portion of her written narrative and her testimony that she was unaware of the threats until her eldest son XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, Ms. XXXX replied that, although she went to the village with her spouse, she was not involved in the meetings and she did not know that her children were in jeopardy at that time. However, this explanation and her testimony are inconsistent with her written narrative which clearly states that she and her spouse were both involved in telling the uncle/brother that they were not interested in subjecting their son to the initiation.7 In fact, in her written narrative, before discussing the "horrors" starting up again when her eldest son XXXX XXXX, Ms. XXXX states that there were many more instances or meetings in which her spouse's uncle/brother tried to convince them (that is, her and her spouse) XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and that all necessary sacrifices must be carried out.

I do not agree with counsel that the RPD's assessment of the issue of when Ms. XXXX became aware of the threats being made by her in-laws was microscopic. The timing of her awareness of these threats is significant to assessing the credibility of her account of the events that led her to leave Nigeria and to claim asylum. In light of Ms. XXXX failure to provide a satisfactory explanation for the above inconsistencies in her evidence, I find that Ms. XXXX was most probably adjusting her testimony at the hearing to make it seem like there had been less of a delay between her awareness of the threats made by her in-laws and her departure from Nigeria. I find that this diminishes her credibility. Extent of the demands/threats made by in-laws

I do not agree with counsel that the RPD erred in finding that Ms. XXXX credibility was compromised due to her inconsistent description of what was involved in the initiation, sacrifice and dedication rituals she described in her written narrative. In her written narrative, Ms. XXXX stated that the rituals entailed going into the evil forest with the chief priest and living there for seven days. She also said it also involved taking a concoction and swearing to the village shrine. However, at the hearing, when the RPD asked her what the dedication or sacrifice involved, she said her son would be killed.

In the appeal memorandum, counsel argues that Ms. XXXX testimony was not inconsistent as she stated in her written narrative that her spouse's uncle/brother told them that, if they did not bring her son for the sacrifice, the son would die in a mysterious way or they could come take him by force. However, this portion speaks to the threats allegedly made by the in-laws if the son was not brought to them for the sacrifice. It still does not explain the inconsistency in Ms. XXXX evidence as to what the sacrifice itself would entail. In her testimony she said that the sacrifice entailed killing her son as a sacrifice to the gods whereas there is no mention of such killing as a sacrifice to the gods in her written narrative.

I agree with the RPD that Ms. XXXX was likely embellishing her claim by testifying at the hearing that the sacrifice being asked of her in-laws entailed the killing of her son as a sacrifice to the gods. While I understand that Ms. XXXX may have been receiving much of this information from her spouse, she is also basing her claim on this information and therefore one would expect a certain degree of precision as to what exactly she is alleging to be involved in the sacrifice or dedication rituals she is alleging. Her failure to provide clear and consistent evidence about what is involved in these rituals, and her apparent embellishment at the hearing, diminish the credibility of her account of the harm that she and her sons risk if they return to Nigeria. Agent of persecution

I agree with counsel that the RPD erred in drawing a negative inference due to the inconsistency in Ms. XXXX evidence as to who exactly she feared in her spouse's family. While it is true that Ms. XXXX stated initially that she feared her spouse's uncle/brother and then later said she feared his whole family, I find that she provided a satisfactory explanation for this differing testimony when she said that she mostly feared the brother but also feared the rest of the family. Incidents after eldest son's tenth birthday

I do not agree with counsel that the RPD erred in finding that Ms. XXXX credibility was diminished by her failure to testify to a significant incident which allegedly occurred in April 2016 and which was the key event that allegedly caused her family to leave Nigeria.

In her written narrative, Ms. XXXX recounted events that occurred in 2014, around the time her eldest son XXXX XXXX. She then alleged that, in April 2016, her spouse's uncle issued an ultimatum that her spouse must either bring the son to him or he would forcibly abduct him. In her written narrative, Ms. XXXX stated that it was at this point that the pressure became unbearable and she and her spouse decided to travel to the US and then to Canada. When the RPD asked Ms. XXXX at the hearing whether she had had any further problems from her in-laws between the time her eldest XXXX XXXX XXXX in 2014 and the time she left Nigeria in XXXX2016, Ms. XXXX said she had not.8 When the RPD asked her questions to understand why her in-laws would not cause problems for Ms. XXXX and her family after 2014, Ms. XXXX said that, personally, she had no problems with the in-laws. She then reiterated that her spouse had not told her about anything until her eldest son XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXMs. XXXX later contradicted herself by saying that she had not said that there were no problems but instead that she herself had not had any problems. When the RPD pressed further to understand what occurred after 2014 that led Ms. XXXX and her family to leave Nigeria, she just said that she was not aware of anything and that, if her spouse went through something with his family, he did not tell her. When the RPD pointed out the portion of her written narrative where she talked about the uncle's ultimatum, Ms. XXXX said that it had been a while since she wrote her narrative and that she believed that she would have the opportunity to explain everything orally before the RPD.9

I agree with the RPD that this is not a satisfactory explanation for why Ms. XXXX in fact did not explain everything orally to the RPD when asked directly about what occurred between 2014 and the time she and her family left Nigeria over two years later. In the appeal memorandum, counsel seeks to blame Ms. XXXX's failure to testify to the ultimatum that made her family leave Nigeria on her XXXX XXXX. I note that Ms. XXXX did not provide this explanation at the hearing. In my view, the evidence does not support that Ms. XXXX mental health issues would explain her failure to testify spontaneously to the key event that made things unbearable for her family and caused them to leave Nigeria. In the XXXX XXXX submitted by Ms. XXXX, the XXXX provided his opinion that she has a XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. While the XXXX XXXX states that persons exposed to trauma often have problems "retrieving specific details from the past," the ultimatum was not a detail but instead the key event that made the pressure unbearable and that made Ms. XXXX and her spouse realize they and their sons were no longer safe in Nigeria.

Therefore, I do not agree with counsel that the psychological report supports the argument that Ms. XXXX's mental health condition would adequately explain her failure to spontaneously remember the key incident that led to her family's departure from Nigeria. I also do not agree with counsel that expecting Ms. XXXX to remember this key incident was an improper memory test. Coincidences in timing

I do not agree with counsel that it was improper for the RPD to question Ms. XXXX about the coincidence in timing between her family's arrival in Canada and the demands that her spouse's family made shortly thereafter. In my view, the RPD had the obligation to provide Ms. XXXX with a chance to address its concerns about this coincidence in timing. It is possible that Ms. XXXX would have information that could satisfactorily explain what appeared to be a suspicious coincidence in timing.

I also do not agree with counsel that the RPD erred in drawing a negative inference based on the coincidence in timing. Ms. XXXX alleged that her in-laws gave her spouse an ultimatum in April 2016, then took no action for the six months it took before they left Nigeria in XXXX XXXX, and then suddenly resumed their threats a couple of weeks after Ms. XXXX and her family arrived in Canada.

In my view, the RPD cannot simply base a negative credibility finding on suspicious coincidences in timing. Coincidences do sometimes occur and therefore the RPD and the RAD must proceed carefully when drawing negative inferences based on coincidences in timing. If the coincidence in timing in this case had been the only credibility concern arising from Ms. XXXX's evidence, it likely would not have been of such significance as to rebut the presumption of truthfulness. However, this coincidence in timing was not the only credibility concern in this case. Credibility assessments are contextual exercises based on a variety of factors. I do not find that the RPD erred in placing some reliance upon this coincidence of events as part of its overall credibility assessment in this case. Spouse's return trips to Nigeria

I do not agree with counsel that the RPD failed to view the actions of Ms. XXXX spouse from his social and cultural background when it drew a negative inference as to credibility based on the fact that Ms. XXXX's spouse returned to Nigeria three times during a time when his life was supposedly also at risk at the hands of his family members.

When the RPD asked Ms. XXXX why her spouse would return to Nigeria if his life was at risk there, she replied that he could not remain in Canada because he has business in Nigeria and he cannot live abroad.10 While Ms. XXXX cannot be responsible for her spouse's actions, I agree with the RPD that her spouse's three trips to Canada and back to Nigeria between December 2016 and December 2018 raised concerns regarding the credibility of Ms. XXXX's claim that she, her spouse, and her sons faced a risk to their lives at the hands of her in-laws during this period of time.

In the appeal memorandum, counsel seeks to provide a further explanation for the trips that Ms. XXXX spouse made between Canada and Nigeria XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. However, this explanation has no actual basis in Ms. XXXX's testimony as Ms. XXXX did not provide the explanation when asked about her spouse's actions by the RPD. Counsel argues that Ms. XXXX spouse was more concerned with his family's safety than his own and that he wanted to resolve things with his family. Counsel argues that the RPD failed to view the actions of Ms. XXXX's spouse from his social and cultural background. I disagree.

According to Ms. XXXX's amended narrative, her in-laws continued to threaten her spouse even after the first RPD hearing in 2017. The documentary evidence shows that her spouse came to Canada twice in 2018 and Ms. XXXX testified that he came to visit in XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, he returned to Nigeria each time, a country where he is allegedly at risk of death, rather than claiming asylum in Canada as his wife and children had done. As noted above, Ms. XXXX cannot be held responsible for her spouse's actions. However, her apparent lack of concern for the risk that her spouse was taking in travelling back and forth between Canada and Nigeria was incompatible with her account of the danger to life that he faced in Nigeria and her credibility was diminished as a result. Failure to claim XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX

I do not agree with counsel that the RPD erred in finding that Ms. XXXX had failed to provide a satisfactory explanation for her failure to claim asylum during her time in the US and that this diminished the credibility of her account of the risk she and her sons faced in Nigeria.

When the RPD asked Ms. XXXX why she had not claimed asylum in the US, she testified that it was never her intention to claim in the US. On the second hearing date, she said that she did not claim asylum in the US because the people her family were staying with in the US had left the country for a vacation and that she had arrived in Canada "before the problem started."

I agree with the RPD that the reasons that Ms. XXXX gave for not claiming asylum in the US were not satisfactory. First, the presence or non-presence of the family she was staying with in the US has no bearing on her ability to claim asylum if her and her son's lives were truly in danger. Second, her claim that the problem had not started contradicts the rest of her testimony which was that the problems with her spouse's family began in 2014 or even earlier and that she feared her in-laws when she and her family left Nigeria XXXX XXXX2016. Indeed, in her written narrative, Ms. XXXX stated that things had become unbearable by that point.

In the appeal memorandum, counsel argues that Ms. XXXX and her children could not stay in the US because they did not have any support there. Counsel argues that Ms. XXXX and her children were away from their home country and had to rely on persons "who were already in the system." It is unclear what counsel means by this last part of the sentence. Ms. XXXX did not say anything in her testimony about having to rely on other persons who were "already in the system." If anything, this explanation appears to suggest that Ms. XXXX and her sons claimed asylum in Canada because they could rely on persons who were already in the system here. This would contradict her testimony that she and her family merely came to Canada for a vacation and they had no intention of claiming refugee status here.

This failure to claim asylum in the US and the inconsistencies in the explanations given for it give rise to a negative inference regarding the credibility of the risk that Ms. XXXX and her family alleged in this case. Delay in claiming asylum

I agree with counsel that the RPD erred in finding that Ms. XXXX's three-week delay in claiming asylum in Canada adversely affected her credibility. I agree with counsel that a three-week delay is not necessarily excessive. Irregularities in documentary evidence

I agree with the RPD's finding that little weight should be given to many of the documents submitted by Ms. XXXX and her sons due to irregularities found on the face of the documents. However, I agree with counsel that the RPD's findings were microscopic with respect to some of the documents. Reports from XXXX XXXX XXXX dated XXXX XXXX, 2017 and XXXX XXXX1, 2017

I agree with counsel that the RPD erred in basing itself on spelling and typographical errors to give little weight to two medical reports stating that Ms. XXXX's husband had XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX2017. However, I note that there are other irregularities on the face of the documents. Both documents essentially say the same thing and therefore it is unclear why both were submitted and why one would be dated March 7, 2017 and the other March 31, 2017. Despite being dated the same month, the documents look completely different one from the other.

In any event, even if I were to overlook these irregularities, I find that any weight that could be accorded to these medical reports does not make up for the serious credibility issues detailed above arising from Ms. XXXX's evidence in this case. This is especially the case because the reports do not assist in repairing any of the credibility problems detailed above. Affidavit of XXXX XXXX dated April 5, 2017

I disagree with counsel that the RPD erred in giving little weight to this affidavit because the declarant did not sign the affidavit. Counsel argues that the fact that the affidavit bears the stamps of the court means that it is presumed genuine. Even if that were the case, this presumption is rebutted by the fact that there was no signature on it. It is not credible that a court would commission an affidavit that was not actually signed by the affiant. Police extract dated XXXX XXXX XXXX 2017

Ms. XXXX submitted a police extract relating to the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX2017. Even if I were to agree with counsel that the error in the date on the police extract should be overlooked due to the fact that Nigeria is a third world country, I do find that any weight that could be given to the report outweigh the credibility problems relating to Ms. XXXX's account of the events that led her to claim refugee protection. E-mails dated between December 13, 2017 and March 30, 2019

I agree with the RPD that any weight that could be given to the emails between Ms. XXXX and her spouse is limited. I note that the emails appear to have been sent for the specific purpose of being used as evidence in this case. For example, Ms. XXXX's spouse starts off one of the e-mails saying, "This is your husband XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX." I do not find it credible that Ms. XXXX would start an email to his wife in this way. She knows who her husband is and there would be no need for him to announce XXXX XXXX XXXX to her in what claims to be a personal email. I find that the emails likely were sent for the purpose of being entered into evidence in this case. Therefore, they should be accorded no weight. Any weight that could be given to the emails does not outweigh the credibility issues detailed above. Affidavits and Police Station Diary extracts related to XXXX XXXX, 2018 incident
I do not agree with counsel that the RPD erred giving little weight to the documents relating to the alleged assault of Ms. XXXX's spouse and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.

In particular, the RPD noted that the affidavit by Ms. XXXX spouse failed to mention that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. While it is true, as noted by counsel, that affidavits should generally be considered for what they say rather than what they do not say, this is not a hard and fast rule. The Federal Court has found it appropriate to draw a negative credibility inference in relation to a document that omits to mention material information.11 That is the case here. One would certainly expect that, if the family of Ms. XXXX spouse killed his father over the dispute over the rituals, he would have thought it important to make some mention of it in his affidavit.

There were additional irregularities on the face of the materials submitted in relation to the June 2018 incident. As noted by the RPD, the same address was provided on the affidavit sworn by Ms. XXXX spouse and the affidavit sworn by an alleged neighbour. When the RPD asked Ms. XXXX why the affidavits indicated that the men lived at the same address, she had no explanation. Counsel did not contest the RPD's finding that this was a further reason to grant little weight to the documents. This finding by the RPD was correct. One would not expect both Ms. XXXX spouse and his neighbour to live at the same address. If there were an explanation for this same address, it should have been easy for Ms. XXXX to provide it at the hearing.

Even if I were to agree with the arguments made by counsel regarding the additional reasons provided by the RPD for discounting the weight accorded to these documents, I find that the irregularity and omission discussed above were sufficient to accord the documents little weight in terms of establishing a forward-looking risk in this case. Psychological report
I do not agree with counsel that the RPD erred in giving little weight to the psychological report submitted by Ms. XXXX in the assessment of the credibility issues described above.

While counsel argues that Ms. XXXX was experiencing XXXX XXXX at the hearing that impacted her testimony and memory recall, the XXXX XXXX does not provide support for this argument. The report states that Ms. XXXX satisfied the criteria XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The report recommended that the RPD allow Ms. XXXX to take breaks during her testimony. I do not agree with counsel that the RPD erred in finding that the report was based on the information Ms. XXXX provided the XXXX Contrary to counsel's arguments that the report was also based on independent testing, the report only states that it was based on an interview of Ms. XXXX. It makes no mention of any independent testing. Given that the RPD correctly found Ms. XXXX not credible in relation to key aspects of her claim, the RPD was correct to question the reliability of the opinions in the report as they were based on an account of events that the RPD found not credible in several key respects.

In addition, the RPD was correct to note that there is a difference between genuine memory loss due to trauma and loss of memory that arises intermittently to explain certain lacunae or inconsistencies in testimony. In this case, Ms. XXXX did not blame very many inconsistencies on any psychological issues. The only times she blamed her state of mind were when she gave inconsistent testimony about the source of the risk she and her family faced and when she failed to testify about the ultimatum given by her brother-in-law in April 2016. While the psychological report states that persons exposed to trauma often have problems "retrieving specific details from the past," neither the reason for the risk faced by Ms. XXXX nor the key event that led her and her family to flee Nigeria are details. They are key parts of Ms. XXXX's account of the risk that she and her sons allegedly face in Nigeria.

For all the above reasons, I do not find that the psychological report establishes that the problems with Ms. XXXX evidence were likely related to any psychological issues she may have been experiencing at the time of the hearing. Overall credibility assessment

While the RPD did err with respect to some of the factors it relied upon to find Ms. XXXX not credible, it was also correct to find that many other factors adversely affected the credibility of Ms. XXXX account of events. In my view, the factors set out above on which the RPD was correct were sufficient to rebut the presumption of truthfulness in this case. Overall, the cumulative effect of the credibility concerns correctly identified by the RPD is that Ms. XXXX and her sons failed to credibly establish that they are either Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.

For the reasons given in the following sections, even if I were to find that Ms. XXXX and her sons had credibly established that they would be at risk of persecution or serious harm if they were to return to their home town, I find that the RPD was correct to find that they have a viable internal flight alternative in Abuja or Enugu. No error in application of internal flight alternative test

The onus is on Ms. XXXX and her sons to demonstrate that they do not have a viable internal flight alternative in Nigeria. The two-pronged test to establish an internal flight alternative is the following.12 (1) The decision-maker must be satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the Appellants would not face a serious possibility of persecution in the internal flight alternative location or a likelihood that they would be subjected personally to one of the types of harm that would make them persons in need of protection there. (2) The conditions in the part of the country under consideration must be such that it would not be unreasonable, in all the circumstances, for the Appellants to seek refuge there. The threshold for unreasonableness is a very high one and requires nothing less than the existence of conditions that would jeopardize the life and safety of a claimant.13 First prong of internal flight alternative test
I do not agree with any of the arguments made by counsel as to why he believes the RPD erred in the application of the first prong of the internal flight alternative test.

Counsel relies on evidence in the National Documentation Package to argue that it is "not inconceivable" that Ms. XXXX brother-in-law would be able to use her Bank Verification Number (BVN) to track her down if she were to return to Nigeria. However, "not inconceivable" is a far lower standard than a serious possibility of persecution, and I agree with the RPD that the available evidence does not establish a serious possibility that Ms. XXXX brother-in-law would be capable of tracking her down using her BVN number. I do not agree that the RPD was approaching counsel's arguments regarding the BVN using western standards. It was instead applying the proper standard of proof to find that, based on the evidence in the National Documentation Package, Ms. XXXX's brother-in-law would not be able to track her down that way.

The National Documentation Package for Nigeria does indicate that there have been some instances of fraud as syndicates attempt to access people's bank accounts and defraud them. However, there was insufficient evidence to establish that Ms. XXXX's brother-in-law has the kind of contacts or resources that would enable him to get access to her BVN and track her down, even if he did somehow become aware that she had returned to Nigeria.

I also do not agree with counsel that the RPD imposed on Ms. XXXX and her sons a higher standard of proof than appropriate by requiring them to provide definitive proof that their agent of persecution would be able to locate them in the internal flight alternative locations. The RPD did not require definitive proof but it did correctly require some kind of persuasive evidence to establish the facts being alleged by Ms. XXXX and her sons on a balance of probabilities and to establish that there was a serious possibility of Ms. XXXX's brother-in-law persecuting Ms. XXXX and her sons in the internal flight alternative locations.

In this case, the RPD found that there was no evidence, other than Ms. XXXX testimony, that her brother-in-law was a retired police officer who had connections that would permit him to track Ms. XXXX and her sons down all over Nigeria. The RPD also found that, in any event, even if Ms. XXXX brother-in-law did have the authority to engage members of the Nigerian police force all over Nigeria to search for Ms. XXXX and her sons, the police would likely be ineffective in finding the claimants. In the appeal memorandum, counsel does not challenge the first finding but only challenges the second by seeking to rely on evidence in the National Documentation Package that the Nigerian police has a command at airports and also has crime reporters. In my view, the RPD did not need to make the alternative finding about the effectiveness of the police force, as it was correct to find that there was insufficient credible evidence in this case to establish that Ms. XXXX brother-in-law was a retired police officer who would be able to enlist the services of police all over Nigeria, including in the internal flight alternative cities, to track Ms. XXXX and her sons down in order to persecute or kill them.

Finally, I do not agree that the RPD erred in noting that Ms. XXXX had no need to advise her brother-in-law or any of her in-laws of her return to the country. Counsel argues that this is tantamount to requiring her to remain in hiding. I do not agree. Refraining from advising your agents of persecution of your return to your home country is not tantamount to living in hiding. In this case, I agree with the RPD that the evidence does not establish that Ms. XXXX brother-in-law or any of her in-laws likely would be aware that she and her sons had returned to Nigeria unless she informed them or someone who would tell them. She and her sons would not be required to live in hiding in the internal flight alternative locations. They simply would have to refrain from informing the agents of persecution where they are.

The case on which counsel seeks to rely is distinguishable as in that case, the RPD expected the claimant not to have any contact with her family when she would require their support due to being a rape victim.14 In the present case, there was no valid reason for Ms. XXXX to inform her in-laws or anyone who would inform them of her and her son's whereabouts.

For all these reasons, I do not agree with the reasons given by counsel as to why he believes the RPD erred in applying the first prong of the internal flight alternative analysis. Having reviewed all of the evidence in this case, I find that the RPD was correct in its analysis under the first prong of the internal flight alternative test. Second prong of internal flight alternative test
I also do not agree with the arguments that counsel makes for why he believes the RPD erred in the application of the second prong of the internal flight alternative test.

At the outset, I note that the reasons given by counsel as to why it would be unreasonable to expect Ms. XXXX and her sons to relocate to one of the internal flight alternatives were not actually reasons given by Ms. XXXX at the hearing. When the RPD asked Ms. XXXX if there were any reasons why she and her sons could not relocate to one of the internal flight alternative cities, she said there was no safety for them anywhere in Nigeria because her brother-in-law could track them anywhere in the country. When the RPD asked whether there were any other reasons she could not relocate to one of the internal flight alternative cities, she said no.15

In the appeal memorandum, counsel makes arguments about indigeneity (ethnic majority status) in Nigeria. Ms. XXXX herself expressed no concern about indigeneity being a factor that would make her relocation to any of the internal flight alternative cities unreasonable. It is true that the National Documentation Package indicates that there is some discrimination based on indigeneity with respect to land ownership, education, government jobs, academic positions, and political positions.16 However, the evidence also indicates that indigene status is less important in big cities such as Lagos or Abuja, than it is in other places, because of the very large non-indigene population in those cities. This was already clear from the evidence contained in the version of the National Documentation Package for Nigeria in place at the time of the RPD hearing.17 It has only been further reinforced in the evidence contained in the version of the National Documentation Package that is currently in place which indicates that non-indigenous people are demographically dominant in cities such as Abuja.18 Therefore, I do not find that the evidence supports counsel's argument that any challenges or discrimination that Ms. XXXX or her sons might face on the basis of being non-indigenes of Abuja that would rise to the level required to place their lives and safety in jeopardy in these cities.

I also do not agree with counsel's argument that "invariably" Ms. XXXX would be discriminated against based on ethnic background in terms of employment, medical care, etc. Again, Ms. XXXX expressed no concern about this being the case. In addition, while the National Documentation Package does indicate that there is some discrimination in terms of hiring practices, in particular, in Port Harcourt and/or Rivers State, the National Documentation Package does not support the argument that Ms. XXXX is likely to experience discrimination in either Abuja or Enugu to such an extent that it would place her or her son's lives and safety in jeopardy.

I also do not agree with counsel's arguments based on Ms. XXXX's alleged status as a newly single woman. Once again, Ms. XXXX raised no concerns in relation to her ability to make a living and find housing as a single woman. I note that I have serious concerns about the credibility of Ms. XXXX claim that her spouse genuinely sought to divorce her a few months before the RPD's re-determination of this case. Nevertheless, even if I accept this to be the case, I find that the evidence does not establish on a balance of probabilities that it would be unreasonable to expect Ms. XXXX and her sons to relocate to Abuja or Enugu.

While the evidence in the National Documentation Packages does indicate that single women do experience some discrimination based on their being single, this discrimination is more prevalent in the northern part of the country rather than in the central or southern parts of the country.19 Also, while the National Documentation Package indicates the existence of gender-based discrimination in the labour market, it also indicates that the likelihood that a woman would encounter such discrimination depends on her particular profile.20 In particular, the evidence indicates that this discrimination is less prevalent for women who have had access to higher levels of education and work experience. Contrary to counsel's arguments, Ms. XXXX is not lacking in work experience. Whether or not she downplayed her position as the CEO of her spouse's business at the hearing, at the very least Ms. XXXX has earned a certificate and worked as a XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. She is also XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. Even if Ms. XXXX were not able to secure employment in these fields, the evidence indicates that women often end up finding jobs in the informal sector XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX which is the kind of work that Ms. XXXX performed XXXX XXXX before she left Nigeria. Finally, I note that, even if I accepted as true that Ms. XXXX and her spouse have separated, there was no evidence in this case that her spouse would refuse to fulfill his financial responsibilities toward his sons.

In terms of discrimination in housing, the National Documentation Package does indicate that it is difficult for female-headed households to find housing in large cities in Nigeria due to discrimination against single women and the high cost of housing. The evidence in the National Documentation Package provides general evidence. In this case, Ms. XXXX did not herself raise any concern about her ability to find housing in either Abuja or Enugu which, in my view, suggests that she believes that she would have the resources or supports in place to ensure that this is the case.

In terms of access to social services, counsel seeks to rely on a part of the National Documentation Package that indicates that the Nigerian government has no general support for women in need. In my view, this is a general issue across the country and there is no evidence that Abuja or Enugu provide less in the way of social services than the rest of the country.

I disagree with counsel that the RPD erred in basing its decision on Ms. XXXX ability to relocate to Canada. Therefore, the Utoh21 case cited by counsel has no relevance to this case. The RPD gave extensive reasons for why the evidence did not establish that there existed cultural, religious, linguistic, economic or other factors that would make it unreasonable to expect Ms. XXXX to relocate to one of the internal flight alternative cities it identified. It did not rest its decision on Ms. XXXX ability to relocate to Canada.

I fail to see the relevance of the Okonkwo22 decision cited by counsel as the facts in that case bear no relationship to this one. In that case, the RPD found that the claimant would be safe in a particular city merely because she had family there. It also based its decision on the claimant's ability to speak English when it was not clear how much English was spoken in the internal flight alternative location. In addition, in that case, the RPD engaged in contradictory reasoning as to whether the claimant could or should live with her family. None of these are factors in this case. Therefore, it is unclear why counsel seeks to rely upon the decision in the present case.

In terms of XXXX, I do not agree with counsel that it was the RPD's onus to demonstrate that Ms. XXXX and her sons would have a viable internal flight alternative in that city. Instead, it was Ms. XXXX and her sons who had the onus of establishing that they did not have a viable internal flight alternative in that city, which they failed to do for all the reasons set out above.

Finally, the RPD's internal flight alternative finding was not based on speculation as was the case in the Loya Dominguez case cited by counsel.23 The RPD's conclusions were well supported by the evidence contained in the National Documentation Package for Nigeria. While it is to be expected to Ms. XXXX and her sons may face challenges relocating to a different city in Nigeria, I agree with the RPD that the evidence does not establish that these difficulties will be of such significance as to put their lives and safety in jeopardy, as is required to find a particular internal flight alternative unreasonable.

For the above reasons, I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.
